paras.text: Plans, Estimating Math, Trade Boundaries and Permits — Audio Lecture

This chapter covers the second biggest block of the trade exam: plans, specifications, and estimating, which is fourteen of the one hundred and ten trade questions. It also covers trade boundaries, meaning what you may not do without a plumbing, electrical, or mechanical license, and the permit and inspection process, which shows up on the business and law side. Everything here keys to the twenty fifteen Michigan Residential Code. Remember that the twenty twenty-one update was stayed by a court in July of twenty twenty-five and never took effect, so if an answer choice smells like the newer national code, treat it with suspicion.

Let's start with reading plans. Floor plans and elevations are drawn at one quarter inch equals one foot. That is the single most tested scale fact. If a wall measures six inches on a quarter-scale plan, multiply plan inches by four and you get twenty-four feet of real wall. Site plans are different. They use an engineer's scale, usually one inch equals twenty feet or one inch equals thirty feet. Details, like a stair connection or a flashing condition, are drawn much bigger, anywhere from three quarters of an inch up to three inches equals one foot.

Know your drawing types. An elevation is a flat picture of the outside face of the house. It shows finishes, window and door openings, the grade line, and the roof slope. A section is a vertical cut through the building, and it is where you find what is inside the wall or floor. Sheathing, studs, insulation, floor to floor heights. If the question asks where you would find the layers of a wall assembly, the answer is the wall section. A detail is a blow-up of one small condition, referenced by a bubble. If you see the number three over the letters A five in a circle, that means detail three, drawn on sheet A five. Sheet prefixes matter too. A is architectural, S is structural, M is mechanical, E is electrical, P is plumbing, and C is civil.

Two rules about conflicts. First, a written dimension always beats a scaled measurement. Never scale a drawing when the number is printed. Second, when the drawings and the written specifications disagree, the specifications generally govern, but the best exam answer is usually to notify the architect and get clarification before you proceed. Remember the division of labor: specs control quality, drawings control quantity and location.

Door and window schedules are tables keyed to marks on the plan. A window called out as three zero five zero is three feet zero inches wide by five feet zero inches high. Width first, then height. A door marked two eight six eight is two feet eight inches by six feet eight inches.

For specifications, know the classic sixteen division C S I MasterFormat. The ones that get tested: division three is concrete, division four is masonry, division six is wood and plastics, division seven is thermal and moisture protection, division eight is doors and windows, division nine is finishes, division fifteen is mechanical, and division sixteen is electrical.

Now the math, and this is where you bank points, because every one of these problems is just a formula. Board feet first. Board feet equals thickness in inches, times width in inches, times length in feet, divided by twelve. A two by six that is ten feet long: two times six times ten is one hundred twenty, divided by twelve is ten board feet. Lumber is priced per thousand board feet. Eight hundred board feet at six hundred dollars per thousand is point eight times six hundred, which is four hundred eighty dollars.

Concrete. Twenty-seven cubic feet make one cubic yard. Length times width times thickness, all in feet, divided by twenty-seven. Convert inches to feet first. Four inches is a third of a foot. So a twenty by thirty slab at four inches is two hundred cubic feet, divided by twenty-seven is seven point four yards. Add five to ten percent waste and round up, so you order eight. On any ordering question, round up. Never order short.

Masonry has two magic numbers. Standard modular brick runs six point seven five bricks per square foot of wall. A thousand square foot wall with a hundred square feet of openings is nine hundred net, times six point seven five is six thousand seventy-five bricks. Standard eight by eight by sixteen block runs one point one two five blocks per square foot. A forty foot wall, eight feet tall, is three hundred twenty square feet, times one point one two five is three hundred sixty blocks.

Roofing is counted in squares, and a square is one hundred square feet. A twenty-four hundred square foot roof is twenty-four squares, and standard three tab shingles run three bundles per square, so seventy-two bundles, plus roughly ten percent waste. Drywall and sheathing come in four by eight sheets of thirty-two square feet. Total your wall and ceiling area, divide by thirty-two, round up, add waste.

Framing counts. Studs at sixteen inches on center: take the wall length in feet, multiply by three quarters, add one, then add extras for corners and openings. The fast field rule is one stud per lineal foot of wall. Joists work the same way: a twenty-four foot run at sixteen on center is twenty-four times point seven five plus one, which is nineteen joists. Plates are three times the wall length, one bottom and a double top.

Excavation. Soil swells when you dig it and shrinks when you compact it. Bank yards are in the ground, loose yards are in the truck, compacted yards are in the fill. Common earth swells about twenty-five percent, so one hundred bank yards becomes one hundred twenty-five loose yards to haul. The trap is shrinkage. If you need one hundred compacted yards and shrinkage is ten percent, you divide by point nine, giving about one hundred eleven bank yards. You divide by one minus the shrinkage. You do not just add ten percent.

Grade and slope. Percent grade is rise over run times one hundred. Two feet of fall in one hundred feet is two percent. A quarter inch per foot is about two percent, and an eighth inch per foot is about one percent, which is your garage floor slope. The code number to know: the ground must fall six inches in the first ten feet away from the foundation, which is five percent, or two percent minimum on pavement.

Stairs are the money problem, and Michigan is different from the national code, so listen carefully. Michigan allows a maximum riser of eight and one quarter inches and a minimum tread of nine inches. The national I R C numbers, seven and three quarters and ten inches, are the trap answers. Here is the method. Total rise divided by the maximum riser, rounded up, gives the riser count. Say the floor to floor rise is one hundred eight inches. Divide by eight point two five and you get thirteen point zero nine. Round up to fourteen risers. The actual riser is one hundred eight divided by fourteen, about seven point seven inches. Treads are always one fewer than risers, so thirteen treads, and at nine inches each, the minimum total run is one hundred seventeen inches. Why round up? Because rounding down to thirteen risers makes each one eight point three one inches, which is over the limit and illegal. One more stair number: risers and treads cannot vary more than three eighths of an inch within a flight.

Now trade boundaries. Your residential builder license lets you build the house, and it lets you coordinate, but it never lets you do plumbing, electrical, or mechanical work. Each trade has its own license, its own permit, and its own inspections. All three trades are now licensed under one law, the Skilled Trades Regulation Act, Act four zero seven of twenty sixteen, which replaced the old separate trade acts. Plumbing goes apprentice, then journeyman at six thousand hours over three years, then master with four thousand more hours over two years. Electrical goes journeyman at eight thousand hours over four years, then master at twelve thousand hours over six years, including two years as a journeyman. In both trades, the contracting business itself needs a separate contractor license, and it must employ a master. A master license alone does not make you a contractor.

Mechanical is the odd one, and it is a favorite exam trap. Under the same Skilled Trades Regulation Act, Michigan licenses the mechanical contractor as a business entity only. There is no individual journeyman or master mechanical license in Michigan. The company designates a qualifying officer and carries classification endorsements for the kinds of work it does. If an answer choice mentions a Michigan master mechanical license, it is wrong. Anyone handling refrigerant also needs federal E P A section six zero eight certification.

The homeowner exemption. A homeowner may do their own trade work on their own primary residence, under their own permit. Rentals are excluded, and a contractor may never work under a homeowner's permit. That is illegal. As the builder, your job is to hire licensed subs, verify their licenses on the LARA website before they start, make sure they pull their own permits, and sequence their inspections.

Permits. The governing law is Act two thirty of nineteen seventy-two, the Stille DeRossett Hale Single State Construction Code Act. No regulated work starts before a permit is issued, ever. But some work is exempt, under section R one zero five point two, and the exemption numbers are pure memorization. A one story detached accessory structure, like a shed, up to two hundred square feet. A fence up to seven feet high. A retaining wall up to four feet, measured from the bottom of the footing, that holds back no surcharge. Sidewalks and driveways not more than thirty inches above grade. Painting, papering, tiling, carpeting, cabinets, and countertops. Above ground prefab pools less than twenty-four inches deep. Window awnings projecting fifty-four inches or less. And decks of two hundred square feet or less that sit no more than thirty inches above grade and do not serve the exit door. Watch the shed trap: two hundred square feet is the current number, one twenty is the old code.

The timelines. The building department has ten business days to issue or deny a permit, fifteen for an unusually complicated building or structure. An issued permit dies if work does not start within one hundred eighty days, or stops for one hundred eighty days. The certificate of occupancy must be issued within five business days of written application, once every permit is finaled, every inspection passed, and every fee paid. Sealed architect plans are not required for one and two family dwellings under three thousand five hundred square feet.

The inspection sequence runs footing and foundation before the pour, waterproofing before backfill, rough framing, then rough electrical, plumbing, and mechanical before anything is covered, then insulation, then drywall, then the four finals, and then the certificate of occupancy. The iron rule: never cover uninspected work. If you do, the inspector can issue a stop work order and make you tear it open. After a stop work order, the only work allowed is what makes the site safe. A knowing violation is a misdemeanor, up to five hundred dollars and up to ninety days. Each knowing violation is a separate offense — and each day counts as a separate offense specifically when you keep working through a stop construction order. Unlicensed residential work draws a separate civil fine of one hundred to five hundred dollars.

Time for the rapid fire recap. Quarter inch equals one foot for floor plans. One inch equals twenty or thirty feet for site plans. Window three zero five zero is three feet by five feet. Board feet is thickness times width times length over twelve. Twenty-seven cubic feet in a yard, five to ten percent concrete waste. Six point seven five bricks per square foot. One point one two five blocks per square foot. A roofing square is one hundred square feet, three bundles per square. A four by eight sheet is thirty-two square feet. Studs at sixteen on center: length times point seven five plus one. Common earth swells twenty-five percent. Grade is rise over run times one hundred, and six inches in ten feet away from the house. Michigan riser eight and a quarter max, tread nine minimum, variance three eighths, treads equal risers minus one, and always round the riser count up. Plumber hours: six thousand journeyman, four thousand more for master. Electrician hours: eight thousand journeyman, twelve thousand master. No individual mechanical license, entity only, with a qualifying officer. Permit exemptions: shed two hundred square feet, fence seven feet, retaining wall four feet, deck two hundred square feet under thirty inches, awning fifty-four inches. Permit in ten business days, dead after one hundred eighty idle days, certificate of occupancy in five business days, sealed plans only at thirty-five hundred square feet and up. And never, ever cover uninspected work.
That is the whole domain. Drill the numbers until they are boring, and this block becomes the easiest fourteen questions on the test.
